screens.heading: Entities: the things you store
screens.body:
An entity is a real-world thing you want to remember — a Student, a Course, a Book. In an ER diagram, each entity becomes a rectangle.

Pick entities by looking for nouns in the problem description. If the business cares about tracking it, it's probably an entity.
screens.keyPoint: Entities are the nouns worth tracking.

check.question: In a library system, which is an entity?

screens.heading: Attributes: the details
screens.body:
Attributes are the properties of an entity — a Student has a name, email, and birth date. They're drawn as ovals attached to the entity rectangle.

The key attribute (like student_id) gets underlined: it uniquely identifies each instance. Choose it carefully — everything else hangs off it.
screens.keyPoint: Attributes describe; the key attribute identifies.

check.question: The key attribute of an entity is…
options: The one that uniquely identifies each instance

screens.heading: Relationships: how entities connect
screens.body:
A relationship captures how two entities interact — a Student enrolls in a Course, an Author writes a Book. In ER diagrams it's drawn as a diamond between the rectangles.

Relationships have names because the verb matters: 'teaches' and 'takes' between Instructor and Course are two different relationships.
screens.keyPoint: Diamonds capture the verbs between entities.

check.question: In an ER diagram, a diamond represents…

screens.heading: Cardinality: how many?
screens.body:
Cardinality says how many of each side can participate. One-to-many: one instructor teaches many courses. Many-to-many: students enroll in many courses, and courses have many students.

One-to-one is rarest: one person has one passport. Getting cardinality right decides where foreign keys go later.
screens.keyPoint: Cardinality = how many on each side.

check.question: Students enroll in many courses; each course has many students. That's…

screens.heading: Reading an ER diagram
screens.body:
Put it together: rectangles are entities, ovals are attributes (underlined = key), diamonds are relationships, and the numbers or crow's-foot marks on the lines show cardinality.

Trace a path with your finger: 'one Department offers many Courses; each Course has many Students.' If you can narrate it, you can read it.
screens.keyPoint: Narrate the diagram out loud to read it.

check.question: Crow's-foot marks on a relationship line show…

screens.heading: Weak entities
screens.body:
A weak entity can't be identified by its own attributes alone — it needs its parent. Order items need their order; a room needs its building.

Weak entities are drawn with double rectangles, and their relationship to the parent is called identifying. Their key borrows from the parent's key.
screens.keyPoint: Weak entities borrow identity from their parent.

check.question: An OrderItem is a weak entity because…
options: It can't be identified without its Order

screens.heading: From ER diagram to tables
screens.body:
Every entity becomes a table; its attributes become columns; the key attribute becomes the primary key. That's the straightforward part.

Relationships become foreign keys: a one-to-many puts the 'one' side's key into the 'many' side's table. Many-to-many needs a whole new junction table holding both keys.
screens.keyPoint: Entities → tables. Relationships → keys (or a junction table).

check.question: A many-to-many relationship between Students and Courses becomes…
options: A junction table holding both keys
